Koeberg Alarm

By: Neil Shaw | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate whether South Africa's only nuclear power station should be operating given the country's unreliable electricity supply.

Unique Selling Point:
Nuclear power stations depend on electricity for cooling, pumps and other key functions... a power cut equals a nuclear meltdown. Koeberg has four levels of back up power, but with Eskom's ongoing power supply issues, there are concerns around Koeberg's nearly-out-of-date power generator (Ankerlig), and technically you just need to lose one back up power level for the plant to be considered unsafe. The Fukishima disaster happened because the tsunami took out the plant's power and back up power (a tsumani could also hit the west coast and engulf Koeberg). New safety recommendations after the Fukushima meltdown of 2011 (including significantly improved measures against power failure) are not being implemented here.

Summary:
Africa's only nuclear power station is the ageing Koeberg plant, located right next to a major city. As Koeberg reaches the end of its lifecycle (around 2024) the government (perhaps to avoid the extremely costly decommissioning process) has started to extend the life of the plant for another 20 years (the "PLEX programme") in a process lacking transparency and likely to be very expensive. But experts warn that this piecemeal overhaul is risky. If anything goes wrong, it would be devastating for Cape Town -- and there is little to no disaster preparedness.

Further information:
- 30 tons of high level nuclear waste is generated every year and stored on site. We'll investigate how safe this is.
- Lack of/poor evacuation plan in case of a nuclear disaster.
- According to the 2020 State of Nuclear Power Report: for the first time in history — renewable sources (excluding hydropower) generated more power than nuclear plants in 2019. And, “Nuclear energy has become irrelevant in the electricity generating technology market."
- Plans to build another nuclear plant at the same site as Koeberg still on the cards. Surely this is unwise for many reasons?
- The 20 year extension plan (PLEX) taking us to 2046, is already underway (new steam generators imported at great cost) in an opaque process.
- Especially given the recent earthquake in Cape Town, why is the Seismic Study not available publically? Are the 900 neoprene pads which the plant sits on as a kind of shock absorber, ok to last a total of 68 years?
- Is there any money for the eventual expensive decommissioning process (estimated conservative cost = 1 billion Euros)? No. Nuclear is not such an economical option after all.
- Can we say for sure that there will be no major political, climatic, seismic or other disruptions for the next 1000 + years? Probably not. The plant can't just be switched it, it has to be decomissioned.
- Is plant maintenance, staff quality, training, and procedures followed to world standards? Ex-staff question this.
- Reference to previous international nuclear disasters: Three Mile Island, Chernobyl, Fukushima, and several smaller-scale incidents.

Script:


Africa’s only nuclear power station started producing electricity for South Africa in 1984.
Koeberg Nuclear plant is only 30 kilometres from the centre of Cape Town, a city that has grown dramatically in the last 40 years. The closest residential suburbs to Koeberg power station, Duynefontein and Melbosstrand, start about five kilometres away.
In the event of an accident -- where an evacuation would be needed -- there would be a tremendous strain on the city’s resources.
The paradox of a nuclear power station, like Koeberg that you see behind me, is that it is dependent on power from the main grid… that power from Eskom is vital for cooling, for pumps, and other key functions. There can be no margin for error. Because a loss of power to a nuclear power station means a nuclear meltdown. 
Reverend Pieter Grove from the United Reformed Church in Kuilsriver, became an anti-nuclear activist in the 1980s when the government started planning a new nuclear power station in the Northern Cape. He started his activism because of the intrinsic fears of nuclear power and lack of nuclear job opportunities for local communities.
Although Eskom says it is repairing the country’s ageing electricity infrastructure, Grove fears it could take only one national outage to cause a disaster at Koeberg.
“The fact that our overall energy distribution in South Africa is becoming increasingly unreliable is a major major danger for Koeberg.” 
Grove took up the civil society seat on the Board of the National Nuclear Regulator for four years from 2004.
It is a crucial seat to represent communities affected by nuclear matters around South Africa. To give them a voice. But the position is currently unoccupied.
Grove has little faith in the back up power systems used in case a national electricity cut starves the plant of the power it depends on.
“Koeberg is supposed to have its own generation that will ensure that nothing can go wrong, but we see the break down of our systems all over South Africa.”
 You spoke about the fact that Koeberg is nearing its end-of-life.
“Koeberg is now almost 40 years old. They want to extend the life of Koeberg for another 20 years. But at some point Koeberg must be decommissioned, because everything will begin to collapse. You cannot maintain such an old thing anymore. What will happen? Where will the money come from simply to decommission this old fossil?”
The recent arrival of new steam generators at Koeberg heralded the government’s plan to extend the plant’s lifespan for a further 20 years.
 “With the plant being very well maintained over the last 36 years of operation, we don’t see any issues that will prevent us from extending the life of the plant for another 20 years, safely. There is a capital investment that goes with it. We’re talking in the order of about 20 billion rand.”
Eskom says that following the Fukushima disaster of 2011, it made improvements to the all-important back up power generators, all of which were destroyed in Japan by the tsunami.
“We have additional back up power. Because one of the key things at Fukushima was they lost their diesels and they couldn’t cool the reactor. So that’s why you see we have the ten generators that we’ve procured.”
Eskom, which is about R450 billion in debt, says it has put aside R16.2 billion for the plant’s eventual complex decommissioning process.
The utility says it runs a tight ship at Koeberg and there’s no need to worry about back-up power in this time of electricity instability.
Peter Geddes was an engineer at Koeberg until 2008 - even then he was worried about safety oversight at the plant. Observing Eskom from a distance today, capacity is his concern.
 “The thing that is really up for question is whether the people that are doing the oversight, which would be our national regulator, is whether they actually do that oversight properly and do all those checks properly.”
At least until 2008 when his term on the Regulator board ended, Reverend Grove feels capacity and transparency were both lacking.
 “Do they have currently the capacity? No. In my opinion. Do they have enough resources? No again. They don’t have.”
Indeed, the National Nuclear Regulator’s 2018/2019 annual report states: “providing effective continuous nuclear safety regulatory oversight to a financially constrained industry in South Africa remains a challenge to the NNR”….
A reminder of the crucial role of a well-capacitated national nuclear regulator was seen in the Japanese government’s report on the Fukushima nuclear disaster. It called the “man-made” disaster the result of a “lack of governance” by “the government, the Japanese power utility Tepco, and the regulators.”
But in their written response to us on these criticisms, the South African National Nuclear Regulator says its “oversight activities are effective and discharged 100% without fear or favour.”
During his tenure as an engineer at Koeberg until a decade ago, Peter Geddes flagged accident preparedness as a main concern.
“If there was a release of gaseous contamination, so the air inside the plant would be contaminated with radioactive iodine, Koeberg does not release that air. It goes through a set of iodine filters to prevent it from being released into the atmosphere… When I was there there was some concern about that testing really being 100% so they could have 100% surety those filters would work in the case of an accident”.
But Eskom says it has a maintenance regime that ensures these filters are tested and checked regularly.  
A nuclear disaster can never be fully mitigated, and Capetonians are not included in Koeberg Nuclear Power Station’s periodic emergency exercises.
The City of Cape Town, in conjunction with Eskom, have been handing out emergency plan information to communities within 16 kilometres of Koeberg on an annual basis for over 20 years.
In the case of a nuclear disaster people in the 16 kilometre zone around the plant would be expected to evacuate following the sounding of public sirens and instructions issued on radio and tv stations.
Potassium iodate tablets which prevent the absorption of radioactive iodine would be distributed by the authorities at pre-arranged locations such as control points.
We phoned schools and fire stations near Koeberg and found they do stock these tablets and that they are replenished with new stock before expiry dates are reached. 
Eskom has general evacuation guidelines, but the City of Cape Town would manage that evacuation. Are they ready?
Alderman J P Smith from the City of Cape Town would be the man in the hot seat to evacuate people within the 16 kilometre zone within 16 hours.
How many people are we trying to move in that short space of time?
“I think it’s 325,92 something residents -- 25 residents, by the last estimate, and those people have to be moved out in 16 hours from the broader area. That is possible for most people to walk out, but people will still be able to use their cars…”
 Peter Becker is an activist who heads up anti-nuclear organisation Koeberg Alert.
“So here we are, day one, in Japan, on our way to Fukushima.”
He visited Fukushima just months after the nuclear meltdown.  
In the northern suburb of Belville, Peter showed us the Velodrome, which could be a mass care centre in case of a Koeberg evacuation.
“In Japan the day after the accident they declared a 20 kilometre evacuation zone, that was mandatory. Police stopped you going into that zone. You had to leave it, and they will not be allowed back into that zone for 100’s of years. So the first thing we can learn is that the 16 kilometre zone is a arbitrary distance. And it’s not sufficient.”
The mandatory evacuation zone in Japan was extended to 30 kilometres a month later -- a point that is not lost on the City of Cape Town, where the CBD is 30 kilometres from Koeberg.
“If your wind is north westerly it will blow your plume of contamination back into the city. You may then have to evacuate many more people.”
“What will happen after the first week? Because this isn’t a temporary zone. Where will they go, where will they live?
It is unclear whether all citizens in Cape Town’s evacuation zone have a tv or radio to be able to receive emergency instructions.
No public fire-drills have been held to test how traffic chaos would be managed.
In case citizens are told to shelter, it is unclear that parents would follow the instructions to “not try to pick up your children at school… [they] will be cared for until you are able to pick them up.”
Residents of nearby Melkbosstrand seemed ill-prepared.
“If something were to go wrong, no I wouldn’t know what to do. I don’t know the protocols, how I would go about it. I would actually be terrified.”
“If a major accident should occur, Cape Town would not be prepared. How would you shift a million people overnight if you have a major accident?”

That is possible for most people to walk out, but people will still be able to use their cars…” Peter Becker is an activist who heads up anti-nuclear organisation Koeberg Alert. “So here we are, day one, in Japan, on our way to Fukushima.” He visited Fukushima just months after the nuclear meltdown. In the northern suburb of Belville, Peter showed us the Velodrome, which could be a mass care centre in case of a Koeberg evacuation. “In Japan the day after the accident they declared a 20 kilometre evacuation zone, that was mandatory. Police stopped you going into that zone. You had to leave it, and they will not be allowed back into that zone for 100’s of years. So the first thing we can learn is that the 16 kilometre zone is a arbitrary distance. And it’s not sufficient.” The mandatory evacuation zone in Japan was extended to 30 kilometres a month later -- a point that is not lost on the City of Cape Town, where the CBD is 30 kilometres from Koeberg. “If your wind is north westerly it will blow your plume of contamination back into the city. You may then have to evacuate many more people.” “What will happen after the first week? Because this isn’t a temporary zone. Where will they go, where will they live? It is unclear whether all citizens in Cape Town’s evacuation zone have a tv or radio to be able to receive emergency instructions. No public fire-drills have been held to test how traffic chaos would be managed. In case citizens are told to shelter, it is unclear that parents would follow the instructions to “not try to pick up your children at school… [they] will be cared for until you are able to pick them up.” Residents of nearby Melkbosstrand seemed ill-prepared. “If something were to go wrong, no I wouldn’t know what to do. I don’t know the protocols, how I would go about it. I would actually be terrified.” “If a major accident should occur, Cape Town would not be prepared. How would you shift a million people overnight if you have a major accident?”

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We investigate whether South Africa's only nuclear power station should be operating given the country's unreliable electricity supply.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Nuclear power stations depend on electricity for cooling, pumps and other key functions... a power cut equals a nuclear meltdown. Koeberg has four levels of back up power, but with Eskom's ongoing power supply issues, there are concerns around Koeberg's nearly-out-of-date power generator (Ankerlig), and technically you just need to lose one back up power level for the plant to be considered unsafe. The Fukishima disaster happened because the tsunami took out the plant's power and back up power (a tsumani could also hit the west coast and engulf Koeberg). New safety recommendations after the Fukushima meltdown of 2011 (including significantly improved measures against power failure) are not being implemented here.
metadata.Summary: Africa's only nuclear power station is the ageing Koeberg plant, located right next to a major city. As Koeberg reaches the end of its lifecycle (around 2024) the government (perhaps to avoid the extremely costly decommissioning process) has started to extend the life of the plant for another 20 years (the "PLEX programme") in a process lacking transparency and likely to be very expensive. But experts warn that this piecemeal overhaul is risky. If anything goes wrong, it would be devastating for Cape Town -- and there is little to no disaster preparedness.
metadata.Further information: - 30 tons of high level nuclear waste is generated every year and stored on site. We'll investigate how safe this is. - Lack of/poor evacuation plan in case of a nuclear disaster. - According to the 2020 State of Nuclear Power Report: for the first time in history — renewable sources (excluding hydropower) generated more power than nuclear plants in 2019. And, “Nuclear energy has become irrelevant in the electricity generating technology market." - Plans to build another nuclear plant at the same site as Koeberg still on the cards. Surely this is unwise for many reasons? - The 20 year extension plan (PLEX) taking us to 2046, is already underway (new steam generators imported at great cost) in an opaque process. - Especially given the recent earthquake in Cape Town, why is the Seismic Study not available publically? Are the 900 neoprene pads which the plant sits on as a kind of shock absorber, ok to last a total of 68 years? - Is there any money for the eventual expensive decommissioning process (estimated conservative cost = 1 billion Euros)? No. Nuclear is not such an economical option after all. - Can we say for sure that there will be no major political, climatic, seismic or other disruptions for the next 1000 + years? Probably not. The plant can't just be switched it, it has to be decomissioned. - Is plant maintenance, staff quality, training, and procedures followed to world standards? Ex-staff question this. - Reference to previous international nuclear disasters: Three Mile Island, Chernobyl, Fukushima, and several smaller-scale incidents.
